findings.confound: downstream compensation (self-repair)
findings.crux: Self-repair/downstream compensation is a phenomenon whereby later layers compensate for an ablated or perturbed earlier component during a causal intervention (e.g. activation patching, zero/mean ablation). The described protocol (PREREG.md; out/results_probe/out/probe_summary_ext_formality.json) contains no ablation or patching step of any kind — it is a passive linear-probe train/test measurement on unperturbed residual activations, plus a permutation-label control. There is no intervened component for any downstream layer to compensate for, so this confound has no mechanism through which to act on this result.

findings.confound: selection bias
findings.crux: Permutation controls (shuffled-train-labels probes) score 0.604/0.719 (mean 0.661) at the same best layer (3) that produced the 1.0000 test accuracy — i.e., a probe trained on scrambled labels still predicts the true held-out labels far above chance. This is the classic signature of selection-bias/leakage in how train and test instances were constructed (surface template/skeleton identity correlating with class assignment) rather than genuine recovery of the formality attribute, and it exceeds the prereg's own gate (0.661 vs allowed 0.153) with clear margin.

findings.confound: readout artifact — task is defined as "whole-message register," so a linear probe on residual activations can achieve perfect accuracy just by reading surface-level formal/casual lexical and syntactic cues (skeleton templates), not by recovering any latent "user preference" representation. The design cannot distinguish a probe that reads token-level style features from one that reads a genuine user-model construct.
findings.crux: out/results_probe/out/probe_summary_ext_formality.json reports permutation controls of 0.604/0.719 (mean 0.661), which exceed the prestated gate |mean-chance| <= 0.153 — i.e., probes trained on shuffled labels still score far above chance on true test labels at the winning layer (layer 3). That is the diagnostic signature of a readout artifact: the "signal" being read is so low-level/surface-bound (register tokens) that even a nonsense-label probe recovers it, meaning the reported test_acc=1.0 cannot be attributed to genuine recovery of a user attribute. The prereg's own decision rule labels this RECOVERED+PERM_ANOMALY = not claimable, and the anchor gate (probe_summary_ALL.json: anchor_in_band=false) additionally voids the extension per QUESTION.md:13-15.

findings.confound: Regime specificity: the claimed "recovery" is tied to the narrow synthetic template regime (formal/casual skeletons, template-disjoint but structurally similar families) rather than to genuine detection of an indirect, planted user-preference signal. This is exactly what regime specificity predicts: strip away the narrow template scaffolding (or test cross-regime) and the recovery would not hold.

findings.confound: Ceiling effect: test accuracy is pinned at 1.0000 (vs chance 0.50) with zero headroom, and — decisively — the permutation-label control (probes trained on shuffled labels) also scores 0.604/0.719 (mean 0.661), well above the 0.50 floor. A properly-behaved null control should sit at chance; instead it sits near the same ceiling region as the real result. This is the signature of a confound where the task's surface-level separability (formal vs casual template skeletons) saturates any linear probe regardless of whether true labels or shuffled labels are used, so 1.0000 test accuracy reflects trivial surface-register separability, not recovery of a "user formality preference."
findings.crux: The permutation control (shuffled labels) scoring 0.604-0.719 instead of ~0.50 chance is the deciding fact: it shows the probe's high accuracy is driven by low-level, label-independent register/surface features at layer 3, saturating the instrument near ceiling for both real and null conditions — exactly what a ceiling/floor confound predicts, and exactly why PREREG's own prestated gate (|mean-chance| <= 0.153) fires and marks the record non-claimable (RECOVERED+PERM_ANOMALY).

findings.confound: Downstream compensation / self-repair describes how later layers/heads reconstruct information after an earlier component is ablated or patched — it is a mechanism that requires a causal intervention (zero-ablation, mean-ablation, activation patching) for downstream units to "compensate" against. The reported experiment is a purely passive linear-probe readout of raw residual activations (test_acc 0.8125 at layer 2, val 1.000) with no ablation, patching, or any perturbation step anywhere in the pipeline (PREREG.md protocol; controls/recheck_rows.py and controls/retrain_probe.sh both operate on raw, unperturbed activations). There is no intervention in this design for any downstream component to be "compensating" for, so self-repair has no causal pathway by which it could inflate or produce the measured probe accuracy. The confound is structurally inapplicable to this measurement.
findings.crux: The protocol never performs an ablation/patching step — it only extracts raw residual activations and trains/evaluates a linear probe on them (out/results_probe/out/probe_summary_ext_native.json, reproduced by controls/retrain_probe.sh ext_native) — so self-repair (a compensatory response to a perturbation) has nothing to compensate for and cannot be the source of the 0.8125 accuracy. (Note: the claim is independently voided by the failed preregistered anchor gate, probe_summary_ALL.json: anchor_in_band=false, and by the acknowledged surface-token confound at layer 2 — but neither of those involves self-repair, which is the confound assigned here.)

findings.confound: Layer selection: "best layer 2 (val 1.000)" implies a sweep over many candidate layers with the max-validation layer reported; a perfect val score on an early layer of a 40-layer model is the signature of multiple-comparisons inflation, not evidence the effect is layer-2-specific or genuine. Only 2 permutation draws (0.521/0.688) calibrate the chance band, a thin basis for ruling out that 0.8125 is the tail of that same selection process.
findings.crux: No committed number reports the full per-layer val-accuracy sweep, so it can't be confirmed whether layer 2's val=1.000 is a real standout or just the max of many near-chance layers picked post hoc — the available facts (implausibly perfect val on an early layer, only 2-sample permutation null, and the independently failed preregistered anchor gate that already voids the extension per QUESTION.md:13-15) are all consistent with selection-over-layers producing the 0.8125 test accuracy rather than the probe reading a genuine user-model representation.

findings.confound: readout artifact: the probe may be reading surface lexical/grammar tokens (fluent vs L1-transfer grammar-error skeletons) directly rather than any internal representation of "user's native-speaker status" as a modeled user attribute.

findings.crux: PREREG.md itself states that for native-speaker status "the cue is necessarily realized in surface text (grammar patterns), so this design cannot in principle separate probe-reads-user-model from probe-reads-surface-tokens for this attribute" — combined with best_layer=2 (an early layer, consistent with surface/lexical encoding rather than an integrated user-model representation), the committed evidence is fully consistent with the 0.8125 accuracy being driven by surface grammar-error tokens rather than any latent user-attribute representation. findings.crux: PREREG.md itself states that for native-speaker status the cue is necessarily realized in surface text (grammar-error vs fluent skeletons), so the design "cannot in principle separate probe-reads-user-model from probe-reads-surface-tokens for this attribute" — meaning any RECOVERED verdict is by the authors' own admission a decodability-of-surface-cue statement, not evidence of a recovered user-attribute representation. findings.confound: Scale incomparability would require comparing quantities measured on different scales/units (e.g., accuracy from a different n, a different chance baseline, or cross-model-size comparison) as if they were commensurable, then attributing an apparent effect to that mismatch.
findings.crux: All the quantities the RECOVERED decision rests on are measured on one identical scale: test_acc=0.8125 and the two permutation controls (0.521, 0.688) are all computed over the same n_test=96 held-out set, against the same chance=0.50 baseline, for the single model/layer (Llama-2-13B-chat, layer 2) named in the claim — there is no second model scale, second n, or rescaled metric anywhere in the evidence for the claim's actual defect (surface-token leakage / gate failure) to be confused with a scale-comparability artifact.

findings.confound: noise floor
findings.crux: The permutation (noise) control was run only twice (0.521, 0.688); one of those two draws (0.688) already exceeds the prestated RECOVERED threshold (0.6531) that the observed 0.8125 is judged against, so with n=2 the upper tail of the noise-floor distribution is uncharacterized and it cannot be established that 0.8125 is reliably above what pure chance can produce on this n_test=96 held-out set.

findings.confound: Ceiling effect at model-selection time: "best layer 2 (val 1.000)" is a saturated/ceiling validation score. If the val split is small or many layers tie at 100%, layer selection loses discriminating power and can pick (or leak toward) whichever layer also happens to score well on test, inflating the reported test_acc=0.8125 beyond true generalization. The reported test metric itself (0.8125, between chance 0.50 and ceiling 1.0, threshold 0.6531 cleared by 0.159) is not itself at a floor/ceiling extreme.
findings.crux: Whether the val=1.000 "best layer" selection reflects a small/tied validation split (many layers saturating trivially, making the selection arbitrary or test-leaky) versus a large, genuinely separating val set — this hinges on n_val and the per-layer val accuracy distribution, neither of which is in the committed evidence (only n_test=96 and chance=0.50 are given).

findings.confound: single-case overfit: only one generator run / one GPU run / one train-val-test split was ever produced. The "best layer" (layer 2) was chosen by maximizing val accuracy, and that val accuracy was a suspicious 1.000 (perfect) — a classic signature of a hyperparameter (layer index) being selected to fit the idiosyncrasies of this one small split rather than a real, layer-stable signal. There is no report of repeated generator seeds, repeated resampled splits, or nested cross-validation to show layer-2's 0.8125 test accuracy is stable across independent instances of the synthetic dataset. The permutation controls (0.521, 0.688) also show run-to-run variance of ~0.17 on a similarly-sized random-label sample, underscoring how much a single n_test=96 draw can swing — and the real test score (0.8125) is not that many such swings above the observed permutation ceiling (0.688).
findings.crux: The layer was selected by best val accuracy, and that val accuracy was a perfect 1.000 — with no independent replicate run (different generator seed / different split) reported to show the resulting test_acc=0.8125 at layer 2 is not just this one split's fit. Absent that replicate, single-case overfit in the layer-selection step remains a live, undecided explanation for the recovered result.
